'''Quantum fingerprinting''' is a proposed technique that uses a [[quantum computer]] to generate a string with a similar function to the [[cryptographic hash function]]. Alice and Bob hold <math>n</math>-bit strings <math> x</math> and <math>y</math>. Their goal and a referee's is to obtain the correct value of <math>f(x,y) = \begin{cases}
  1 & \text{if } x = y, \\
  0 & \text{if } x \neq y. \\
 \end{cases}</math>. To do this, <math>2^{n}</math> quantum states are produced from the O(logn)-qubit state fingerprints and sent to the referee who performs the [[Swap test]] to detect if the fingerprints are similar or different with a high probability.<ref name="BCWW01">
{{cite journal
  | author = [[Harry Buhrman]], [[Richard Cleve]], [[John Watrous (computer scientist)|John Watrous]], [[ Ronald de Wolf]]

If unconditional guarantees of security are needed, and if it is impractical for the communicating parties to arrange to share a secret that can be used in a [[Carter–Wegman MAC]], this technique might one day be faster than classical techniques given a [[quantum computer]] with 5 to 10 [[qubit]]s.  However, these circumstances are very unusual and it is unlikely the technique will ever have a practical application; it is largely of theoretical interest.
